page: Google Cloud Platform m4-megamem-28 belongs to the Memory Optimized server family, engineered for workloads requiring high memory capacity relative to compute resources. The instance is built on the x86_64 architecture and provides 28 dedicated vCPUs alongside 372.0 GB of system memory, delivering approximately 13.29 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include integrated graphics processing units, operating with 0 GPUs.

Storage architecture for the m4-megamem-28 relies entirely on external network storage, as the configuration lists no bundled local storage. Network connectivity provisions do not include complimentary public IPv4 addresses, necessitating external configuration for external routing. The dedicated CPU allocation ensures consistent processor availability without hypervisor core contention.

From a resource efficiency perspective, the high RAM-to-vCPU ratio targets environments where memory footprint exceeds compute demands, preventing the unnecessary over-provisioning of processor cores. The primary operational tradeoffs stem from the absence of bundled local storage, requiring network block storage for persistence. The instance fits large in-memory databases, memory-intensive caching systems, large-scale data analytics, and enterprise transaction processing where memory capacity is the main bottleneck.
description: Google Cloud Platform m4-megamem-28 is a memory-optimized virtual machine designed for memory-intensive enterprise tasks. Powered by the x86_64 architecture, this instance features 28 dedicated vCPUs paired with 372.0 GB of system memory, yielding approximately 13.29 GB of RAM per vCPU. It operates without hardware GPU accelerators and includes no bundled local storage, relying on external network-attached storage solutions for persistent data management. In addition, zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned by default. By concentrating a massive memory capacity onto 28 dedicated cores, m4-megamem-28 offers efficient resource utilization for workloads constrained by RAM rather than raw processing power. It is well-matched for large in-memory databases, distributed caches, complex real-time analytics engines, and enterprise resource planning software requiring substantial physical memory without requiring excessive vCPU counts.
